subject: physics
title: Capacitance
key_idea: Capacitance is the charge stored per volt, C = Q/V, measured in farads. For parallel plates it depends on the area, the separation and the material between the plates. Capacitors add in parallel and combine as reciprocals in series.

blocks.text: A capacitor stores charge on two conducting plates separated by an insulator. Capacitance measures how much charge it stores for each volt across it.

items.meaning: The charge stored on one plate per unit potential difference across the capacitor.
The unit of capacitance. One farad stores one coulomb of charge per volt, 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹.

blocks.label: Capacitance
where: Q = magnitude of the charge on one plate (C)
V = potential difference across the capacitor (V)

items: One plate carries +Q and the other −Q, so the capacitor as a whole has no net charge.
For a given capacitor, C is fixed, so the charge stored is directly proportional to the p.d.
A graph of Q against V is a straight line through the origin. Its gradient is the capacitance.
The farad is very large. Real capacitors are measured in μF, nF and pF.
Capacitance is charge stored per unit p.d., C = Q/V.
The unit is the farad, 1 F = 1 C V⁻¹.
Q is the charge on one plate, not the total on both.

blocks.text: The capacitance of two parallel plates depends on the plate area, the gap between them and the insulator in the gap.

items.meaning: A constant, 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m, for a vacuum (air is almost the same).
A property of the insulator. ε = εᵣε₀.
The ratio ε/ε₀. It is also called the dielectric constant and is never less than 1.

blocks.label: Parallel plate capacitor
where: A = area of overlap of the plates (m²)

items: Capacitance is directly proportional to the plate area A.
Capacitance is inversely proportional to the separation d.
Replacing air by an insulator with relative permittivity εᵣ multiplies the capacitance by εᵣ.

diagram.alt: A slider activity. Change the plate area, the plate separation and the insulator between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor and watch the capacitance change.

items: C = ε₀εᵣA/d for parallel plates.
Bigger plates, a smaller gap or a higher εᵣ all increase the capacitance.

blocks.text: A single conducting sphere also stores charge. Its capacitance is found from its potential, with the other 'plate' taken as far away at zero potential.

items.text: At the surface of a sphere of radius R carrying charge Q, V = Q / (4πε₀R).

items: The capacitance depends only on the radius, not on the charge.
Even a sphere of radius 1 m has a capacitance of only about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ F.
An isolated sphere has C = 4πε₀R.
It follows from V = Q/(4πε₀R) and C = Q/V.

sections.heading: Capacitors in parallel and in series

blocks.text: Combining capacitors changes the total capacitance. Each rule follows from C = Q/V.

items.text: Every capacitor is connected across the same supply, so each has the same p.d. V.
The total charge is Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + … and each Q = CV.
CV = C₁V + C₂V + …, so the V cancels.
The joined plates between capacitors are isolated, so each capacitor stores the same charge Q.
The supply p.d. is shared: V = V₁ + V₂ + …
Q/C = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂ + …, so the Q cancels.

items: In parallel the total is larger than any one capacitor.
In series the total is smaller than the smallest capacitor.
In series the smaller capacitance has the larger p.d., because V = Q/C with the same Q.

diagram.alt: A calculation. Find the combined capacitance of two capacitors in series.
diagram.question: Two capacitors of {c1} μF and {c2} μF are connected in series. Calculate their combined capacitance in μF.

items: Parallel: capacitances add and the p.d. is the same.
Series: reciprocals add and the charge is the same.
Both rules come from C = Q/V.

checks.q: A 470 μF capacitor is connected across a 12 V supply. Calculate the charge stored on one plate.
The separation of the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is doubled and the air is replaced by an insulator with relative permittivity 3. State and explain the effect on the capacitance.
checks.a: C is proportional to εᵣ/d. Doubling d halves C and εᵣ = 3 triples it, so the capacitance increases by a factor of 1.5.

checks.q: A 6.0 μF capacitor and a 3.0 μF capacitor are connected in series across a 12 V supply. Calculate the combined capacitance and the charge on the 6.0 μF capacitor.
checks.a: 1/C = 1/6.0 + 1/3.0 = 1/2.0, so C = 2.0 μF. Q = CV = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 12 = 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ C. The charge is the same on each capacitor in series.

blocks.text: Many insulators are made of polar molecules. Each has one end slightly positive and the other slightly negative.

items.text: The molecules point in random directions, so there is no overall effect.
The field between the charged plates makes each molecule rotate, with its negative end towards the positive plate.
Opposite charge appears on the faces of the insulator, next to each plate. It partly cancels the field.
The p.d. for the same charge on the plates is smaller, so C = Q/V is larger.

items: Polar molecules rotate to line up with the field.
The insulator's surface charges reduce the field, so more charge fits on the plates for each volt.
In a steady d.c. circuit no current flows through a fully charged capacitor, so it acts like a break in the circuit.
A resistor in series with a fully charged capacitor has no current, so it has no p.d. across it.
While a capacitor is charging, a current flows and the resistor does have a p.d. (see charging and discharging).
A capacitor in parallel with a resistor has the same p.d. as that resistor.

blocks.text: Investigating capacitors in series and parallel

items: Connect the capacitors to a d.c. supply, in series and then in parallel.
Use a voltmeter to measure the p.d. across each capacitor and across the combination.
Use an ammeter in the circuit to see the charging current fall to zero when the capacitors are fully charged.
Compare the measured p.d. values with those predicted by the combination formulae.
A charged capacitor blocks steady current.
Meters let you check the series and parallel rules.
